isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.answer: The four phases are preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; and post-incident activity. You contain first because cutting the compromised system off stops the attack spreading and stops the attacker steering it while you work out how to remove them. You leave it powered on because memory holds running processes and live network connections, evidence that is lost the moment the power goes. You eradicate before recovering so restored systems are not reinfected through a leftover foothold. A playbook is the written plan for one kind of incident, such as ransomware, set out as concrete steps with named owners. The lessons-learned review in the final phase feeds back into preparation, improving the plan and playbooks.

isc2.cc.d5.logging-monitoring::isc2.cc.d.answer: Log successful and failed sign-ins with their source, privilege changes such as new accounts or admin-group additions, configuration changes like firewall rules or installed software, access to sensitive data, and security tools' own alerts. A SIEM collects logs from across the organisation, normalises them into one format, correlates events from different sources and raises alerts when a rule matches. Clocks must be synchronised to one time source or events cannot be put in order, and logs must be shipped to a separate protected store so an intruder with admin rights cannot erase them; keep them for a set retention period. For a suspected brute-force attack, establish where the attempts came from, how many there were, which accounts were tried, over what time span, and whether any attempt from that source succeeded.
